text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft, a few questions. Each answer would change what the letter says.

1. **Names and details.** I need your name and title, the farm's name and town, Tomás's last name, and who the letter goes to (a named admissions contact, or "Admissions Committee"). Did the college send a form or specific questions the letter should answer?

2. **What the mastitis catches were worth.** Do you have a number for those 9 early cases: cows saved, treatment costs or discarded milk avoided, or how that winter compared with earlier ones? An admissions reader can't tell how much 9 cases matters, so a figure turns it into evidence.

3. **The 5-week absence.** The college won't know about it unless you bring it up. But if the letter says "missed 2 shifts in 3 years" and leaves out the 5 weeks, the record looks better than it was. I'd suggest one honest line, something like "apart from a family medical emergency, he has missed two shifts in three years." What do you want to say? And did he come back on the date he said, or did anything else happen around it that you'd want included, like whether he helped arrange cover?

4. **Written English.** The reader will wonder whether he can keep up with the coursework. Is there anything that shows his writing at work, like entering records in the herd software or writing notes for the vet? Have you seen him improve since he started the night class?

5. **What you can commit to.** Would you hire him back, or keep him on part-time, during or after the program? Do you know what he wants to do with the degree? If you can say "we'd hire him back," that's one of the strongest lines a reference can have. Only include it if it's true.

1. Mike Hollis, farm manager, Hollis Dairy. I'd rather not put the town in. His full name is Tomás Reyes. I don't have a named contact, so "Admissions Committee" is fine. No form or questions that I know of. It goes in through the college's online portal and is due February 1.

2. The vet said catching those cases early saved us about $8,000.

3. Use your line. Before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would.

4. He enters stuff in the herd software, but I don't know that it shows much writing. I couldn't tell you if he's improved since the night class. He did fail the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

5. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program. I can also take a phone call from the committee at 555-0187. I can't pay any of his tuition. I don't know what he wants to do with the degree.

Here's the letter. It's about 350 words, so it fits on one page.

<final_document>
Dear Admissions Committee,

I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow operation, and I am writing to recommend Tomás Reyes for your two-year agricultural technology program. Tomás has worked for us for three years, since he was 19. The best evidence I can give you of how he will do in your program is what he already does with farm technology every week.

Tomás learned our herd management software on the job, and he now uses it to flag sick cows for our veterinarian. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early. Our vet estimates that catching those cases early saved us about $8,000. Using herd data to make decisions about animal health is the kind of work your program trains people for, and Tomás is already doing it.

He is also someone you can count on. He runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. Apart from a family medical emergency, he has missed two shifts in three years. That emergency was last summer, when his father became seriously ill in Mexico and Tomás was away for five weeks. Before he left, he arranged for his cousin, a former employee of ours, to cover his shifts, and he came back on the day he said he would.

I want to be straightforward about one thing. Tomás's spoken English is stronger than his written English, and he knows it. He is taking a night class to improve his writing, on his own time, while still working the early milking shift. He learned our software by sticking with it, and I expect he will handle written coursework the same way.

I will keep his job open part-time on weekends while he is in the program. I would be glad to talk with anyone on the committee about him. You can reach me at 555-0187.

I recommend Tomás for your program.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
555-0187
</final_document>

A few things to check before you upload it by February 1:

- **The written English paragraph.** I included it because the committee will probably see his writing in the application anyway. It's better that they hear about the night class from you than wonder about it. If you'd rather not bring it up, you can delete that paragraph and nothing else needs to change.
- **What I left out.** I didn't mention the failed-then-passed safety test. It does show he keeps at things, but it also puts a failed written test in front of an admissions committee. I also left out that he gave only 2 days' notice before the trip. Since he arranged cover and came back on time, the short notice didn't change the outcome. Add either one back if you think it belongs.
- **Dates and letterhead.** I didn't put a date on it. If the portal or your letterhead calls for one, add it at the top.
